title: Chapter 3.  Modern History - British Raj, Capital Shift & Independence

blocks.content: Delhi's modern history chapter is dominated by one pivotal, heavily-tested event: the 1911 Delhi Durbar announcement shifting British India's capital from Calcutta to Delhi, and the subsequent construction of New Delhi. Combine this with the 1857 Revolt's Delhi chapter and Partition-era demographic upheaval for full coverage.
Late Mughal Decline & the Revolt of 1857

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Revolt of 1857 marked the final decline of the Mughal Empire and the consolidation of the British Raj.
The capital of British India was shifted to Delhi during the famous Delhi Durbar of 1911.
1947 marked India's Independence and Partition, triggering massive demographic and structural transformations in Delhi.

blocks.content: By the early 19th century, Mughal authority had shrunk to a nominal presence in Delhi under British protection, with the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, holding largely ceremonial power while the British East India Company controlled the wider region.

During the Revolt of 1857, Delhi became a major centre of the uprising: sepoys who had rebelled at Meerut marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar the symbolic leader of the rebellion; British forces recaptured the city after prolonged fighting, notably at the Delhi Ridge (Northern Ridge), by September 1857.

Following the revolt's suppression, Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to Rangoon (Burma), formally ending Mughal rule; the British Crown assumed direct control of India in 1858, ending East India Company rule.

★ EXAM POINT: The Northern Ridge in Delhi (part of the wider Delhi Ridge system covered in Chapter 1) was the key British military encampment and battle site during the 1857 siege of Delhi - a geography-history crossover fact worth remembering.
The 1911 Delhi Durbar & Shift of Capital

At the Delhi Durbar of 12 December 1911, held to mark the coronation of King George V and Queen Mary as Emperor and Empress of India, the British Government formally announced the transfer of British India's capital from Calcutta to Delhi - a decision driven by Delhi's historic-symbolic status as an ancient seat of Indian empires and by growing nationalist agitation in Bengal (following the 1905 Partition of Bengal), which the British hoped to defuse by relocating the capital.

The foundation stone of the new capital was laid at the Durbar itself; the site was subsequently shifted from the original Durbar ground (in North Delhi, later marked by the Coronation Memorial) to a new location further south, around Raisina Hill.

British architects Sir Edwin Lutyens and Sir Herbert Baker were commissioned to design the new capital, 'New Delhi', blending classical European architectural forms with Indian decorative elements (chhatris, jaalis, and other motifs) - a style often termed 'Indo-Saracenic' or, more specifically for this project, 'Delhi Order' architecture.

New Delhi was formally inaugurated on 13 February 1931 by Viceroy Lord Irwin, after roughly two decades of planning and construction, becoming the seat of British India's government just 16 years before Independence.

cells: Delhi Durbar - capital shift from Calcutta to Delhi announced
1911 (at the Durbar; site later relocated to Raisina Hill)
Sir Edwin Lutyens (principal planner; Rashtrapati Bhavan) and Sir Herbert Baker (North & South Blocks/Secretariat buildings)

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: A frequently tested trap: the Durbar ANNOUNCEMENT was in 1911, but New Delhi was only formally INAUGURATED in 1931 - a 20-year construction gap that examiners like to test by asking for either date alone.

New Delhi became the capital of independent India upon Independence on 15 August 1947; the Constituent Assembly met at what is today Sansad Bhavan (Parliament House, built as part of Lutyens' New Delhi and originally the Imperial Legislative Council building).

items: The year 1911 is frequently asked regarding the transfer of the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi during the Delhi Durbar.
Key events surrounding the Revolt of 1857 and the subsequent end of Mughal rule are vital topics for Modern Indian History.

blocks.content: Partition brought a massive demographic transformation to Delhi: large numbers of Hindu and Sikh refugees arrived from West Punjab and Sindh (now in Pakistan), while a substantial Muslim population left Delhi for Pakistan - permanently reshaping the city's social geography, with refugee resettlement colonies (such as Lajpat Nagar, Rajinder Nagar, and parts of West Delhi) established specifically to house incoming refugees.

This influx roughly doubled Delhi's population within a few years of Independence and cemented its transition from a primarily Mughal-British administrative-heritage city into modern India's fastest-growing metropolitan capital.

items: 1857 Revolt: Delhi was a major centre; Bahadur Shah Zafar proclaimed symbolic leader; British recaptured Delhi via the Northern Ridge, Sept 1857; Zafar exiled to Rangoon.
1911 Delhi Durbar (12 Dec 1911): capital shifted from Calcutta to Delhi, announced during George V's coronation durbar.
New Delhi designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens & Sir Herbert Baker; formally inaugurated 13 February 1931.

Partition (1947) brought a massive refugee influx from West Punjab/Sindh, roughly doubling Delhi's population and reshaping its social geography (e.g. Lajpat Nagar, Rajinder Nagar resettlement colonies).
